title: Brick
full_review:
If you've never heard of a "yegg" or think the term "duck soup" refers to the Marx Brothers' film, you may have a hard time following along with some of the exchanges in "Brick" (Focus), a gritty low-budget murder mystery which gives the high-school movie a film-noir twist, by combining the teen and classic detective genres.

But translation difficulties aside -- you'll have to adjust your ears to the pulp-flavored slang (guns are "gats," cops are "bulls" and "taking a powder" means "making an exit") spoken in clipped dialogue -- the movie is clever in its fusion of old and new.

Set in Southern California, the story's gumshoe is a high-school loner, Brendan (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), whose obsessive search for Emily (Emilie de Ravin), his missing ex-girlfriend, leads him to uncover a dangerous maze of drugs, jealousy and deception, with a list of suspects that includes her junkie boyfriend (Noah Segan), a manipulative socialite (Nora Zehetner), a drug dealer (Lukas Haas) and a volatile thug (Noah Fleiss).

Inspired by the crime novels of Raymond Chandler and Dashiell Hammett, director Rian Johnson's hard-boiled hybrid -- with its shaggy-haired shamus and student body of heavies and femme fatales -- proves intriguing despite its modest scale.

The film contains some violence, including several rough beatings and a shooting, recurring drug content, unflattering portrayal of authority figures, underage drinking and smoking, and sporadic crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
